issues.description: Attribute type mismatch: the problem statement UML declares numberOfInscribedStudents and numberOfGuestStudents as double, but the solution defines these attributes as int. Students will be unsure whether to implement these fields as double or int and may implement constructors/getters/setters with the wrong types.
issues.suggestedFix: Make the attribute types consistent across problem statement, template and solution. Either change the UML and problem text to declare the two student count attributes as int, or update the template and solution to use double and adjust related methods accordingly (e.g., return types/calculations).

issues.description: Constructor parameter type mismatch: the problem describes a constructor that initializes attributes following the UML (which uses double for the student counts), but the solution constructor signature uses int parameters for those values. This inconsistency can confuse students when implementing the constructor signature and parameter types.
issues.suggestedFix: Align the constructor parameter types with the attribute types declared in the problem UML. If the UML is corrected to use int for student counts, update the problem text to specify int. If double is intended, change the solution and template constructor parameters to double and update assignments and method implementations accordingly.

issues.description: Inner inconsistency in the problem UML: the UML declares numberOfInscribedStudents and numberOfGuestStudents as double but declares getTotalNumberOfStudents() to return int. This contradiction leaves students uncertain about expected return types and numerical precision.
issues.suggestedFix: Clarify the UML and problem text so types are consistent: either make the student-count attributes int (and keep getTotalNumberOfStudents() returning int) or keep them double and change getTotalNumberOfStudents() to return double (and update descriptive text/examples).
